title: Why You'd Never Survive on Mars
screen_title: Why You'd Never Survive on Mars
subtitle: The planet that looks like home, and isn't
yt_title: Why You'd Never Survive on Mars (Without a Lot of Help)
intro: Mars looks almost friendly: deserts, mountains, sunrises, a day just a little longer than ours. So why would it kill you so quickly? We land on the Red Planet and face its thin air, deadly cold, poisonous dust, radiation and planet-wide dust storms, climb the tallest volcano in the solar system, and ask whether humans could ever live there.
questions: Would you take a one-way ticket to Mars?
What would you miss most about Earth?
What should we never get close to next?

segments.chapter: The planet that looks like home
segments.text: Of all the planets, Mars looks the most like home. Deserts, mountains, canyons, even sunsets. A day there lasts just a little longer than ours. So why would it kill you in less than a minute?

files: Mars - August 30 2021 - Flickr - Kevin M. Gill.png

segments.text: Welcome to Next Stop: Universe. If you enjoy calm, easy-to-follow journeys through space, tap subscribe. Today we land on Mars, and find out what would get you first.

files: A Dark Sky Full of Light (horalek-vst-milky-way).jpg
visual.query: A Dark Sky Full of Light (horalek-vst-milky-way)

segments.text: First, getting there. Mars and Earth line up for a good launch only about once every twenty-six months.
segments.headline: Once every 26 months

segments.text: Even then, the trip takes around seven months. The Apollo astronauts reached the Moon in three days. This is seven months, with no way to turn back.

visual.label: from Earth to Mars
visual.sub: Apollo reached the Moon in 3 days

segments.text: And the whole way, you're outside Earth's protective magnetic field, bathed in radiation from the Sun and from deep space.
segments.headline: Radiation on the way

segments.text: NASA's Curiosity rover measured the radiation during its trip. The flights there and back alone could add up to more than NASA's whole career limit for an astronaut.
Now imagine you've landed. You open the hatch and step outside, in normal clothes. What happens?
segments.headline: Opening the door

segments.text: Mars's air is less than one percent as thick as Earth's. And almost all of it is carbon dioxide.
With so little pressure, the air rushes out of your lungs. The water in your tongue and eyes starts to boil, even though it's freezing cold. In about fifteen seconds, you'd pass out.

files: Mars - August 30 2021 - Flickr - Kevin M. Gill.png
visual.query: Mars - August 30 2021 - Flickr - Kevin M. Gill

segments.headline: 15 seconds

segments.text: The average temperature is about minus sixty degrees Celsius. At night it can drop below minus one hundred.

On a summer afternoon near the equator, the ground can reach around twenty degrees Celsius. But just above it, the thin air stays freezing. Your feet would feel spring while your head felt deep winter.

files: Spanning the Delta of Jezero Crater on Mars (PIA25022).jpg
visual.query: Spanning the Delta of Jezero Crater on Mars (PIA25022)

segments.headline: Warm feet, frozen head

segments.text: So here's my first question. If you were offered a one-way ticket to Mars, would you take it? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: Would you take a one-way ticket to Mars?

segments.text: Let's say you have a spacesuit. You're safe from the air and the cold. Now look down.
segments.headline: Look down

segments.text: Mars is red because its dust is full of iron oxide. Rust. And the dust is everywhere.

files: Mars - August 30 2021 - Flickr - Kevin M. Gill.png
visual.query: Mars - August 30 2021 - Flickr - Kevin M. Gill

segments.headline: A rusty planet

segments.text: In twenty oh eight, NASA's Phoenix lander found chemicals called perchlorates in the soil. They're toxic to humans, and can harm the thyroid gland.

files: South Polar Cap of Mars during Martian South summer 2000.jpg
visual.query: South Polar Cap of Mars during Martian South summer 2000

segments.headline: Toxic soil

segments.text: The dust is also very fine and sharp. It would cling to your suit, get inside your base, and into your lungs.
And sometimes, the dust takes over the whole planet.

files: Mars - August 30 2021 - Flickr - Kevin M. Gill.png
visual.query: Mars - August 30 2021 - Flickr - Kevin M. Gill

segments.headline: Dust storms

segments.text: In twenty eighteen, a dust storm grew until it covered nearly all of Mars. It blocked the sunlight for months, and the solar-powered Opportunity rover went silent forever, after almost fifteen years of exploring.
segments.headline: Opportunity's last storm

segments.text: But here's a surprise. In movies, Martian storms knock people over. In reality, the air is so thin that even a hundred kilometer an hour wind would feel like a gentle breeze. The real danger is the darkness and the dust.
segments.headline: A gentle wind

segments.text: And then there's the radiation, every single day. Mars lost its global magnetic field billions of years ago.
segments.headline: No magnetic shield

segments.text: Without that shield, the solar wind slowly stripped away most of its air. And today, radiation from space hits the surface directly.

files: Mars - August 30 2021 - Flickr - Kevin M. Gill.png
visual.query: Mars - August 30 2021 - Flickr - Kevin M. Gill

segments.headline: Stripped by the Sun

segments.text: On the surface, you'd absorb radiation many times faster than on Earth. Long stays would raise the risk of cancer and other illness.
Future explorers might have to live underground, or under thick walls of Martian soil, just to stay safe.
segments.headline: Living underground

segments.text: But Mars is also a place of record-breaking wonders.
segments.headline: Olympus Mons

segments.text: Olympus Mons is the tallest volcano in the solar system, about twenty-two kilometers high. Around two and a half times taller than Mount Everest.
It's so wide, about six hundred kilometers, that if you stood on its slopes, the peak would be hidden beyond the horizon. You might not even know you were on a mountain.

files: Olympus Mons - NASA Mars Global Surveyor (54542130265).png
visual.query: Olympus Mons - NASA Mars Global Surveyor (54542130265)

segments.headline: Too big to see

segments.text: At the top is a giant crater, a caldera, deep enough to swallow entire cities.

files: Olympus Mons Caldera - ESA Mars Express (54041132578).png
visual.query: Olympus Mons Caldera - ESA Mars Express (54041132578)

segments.text: And then there's Valles Marineris, a canyon system about four thousand kilometers long. On Earth, it would stretch almost all the way across the United States.

files: PIA00005 Oblique View of Valles Marineris.jpg
visual.query: PIA00005 Oblique View of Valles Marineris

segments.headline: Valles Marineris

segments.text: In places, it's about seven kilometers deep. Four times deeper than the Grand Canyon.
Gravity on Mars is only about thirty-eight percent of Earth's. You could jump almost three times higher.
segments.headline: 38% gravity

segments.text: And at sunset, the sky turns blue around the Sun, the opposite of Earth. Fine dust scatters blue light forward, toward your eyes.
segments.headline: Blue sunsets

segments.text: Billions of years ago, Mars was a very different place. Rivers flowed, and lakes filled its craters.

files: Spanning the Delta of Jezero Crater on Mars (PIA25022).jpg
visual.query: Spanning the Delta of Jezero Crater on Mars (PIA25022)

segments.headline: Rivers and lakes

segments.text: NASA's Perseverance rover landed in Jezero crater, an ancient lake, to look for signs of past life.
segments.headline: Perseverance

segments.text: In twenty twenty-four, it found a rock with tiny leopard spots. In twenty twenty-five, scientists called it a potential sign of ancient life. Potential means maybe, not proof.

files: 1-PIA26368-Perseverance Finds a Rock with Leopard Spots-annotated.png
visual.query: 1-PIA26368-Perseverance Finds a Rock with Leopard Spots-annotated

segments.headline: Leopard spots

segments.text: Perseverance even carried a little helicopter, Ingenuity, the first aircraft to fly on another planet. It made seventy-two flights.
segments.headline: The first flight on Mars

segments.text: Life there would feel strange in other ways too. A Martian day, called a sol, lasts twenty-four hours and thirty-seven minutes. Almost like home.

files: Spanning the Delta of Jezero Crater on Mars (PIA25022).jpg
visual.query: Spanning the Delta of Jezero Crater on Mars (PIA25022)

segments.headline: A sol

segments.text: But a Martian year lasts six hundred eighty-seven Earth days. Each season lasts about twice as long as ours.
Perseverance carried microphones. They revealed that on Mars, sound is quieter, and high-pitched sounds travel a little faster than low ones. A conversation would sound oddly muffled.
segments.headline: Sound on Mars

segments.text: Whirling dust devils, several kilometers tall, sweep across the plains. Some of them even cleaned the dusty solar panels of NASA's rovers.

files: Mars - August 30 2021 - Flickr - Kevin M. Gill.png
visual.query: Mars - August 30 2021 - Flickr - Kevin M. Gill

segments.headline: Dust devils

segments.text: And calling home would be slow. A radio message takes between about three and twenty-two minutes to reach Earth, depending on where the planets are.

visual.label: for a message to reach Earth

segments.text: Mars also has two small moons. The bigger one, Phobos, is slowly spiraling inward. In tens of millions of years, it will break apart, and may form a ring around Mars.
segments.headline: A doomed moon

segments.text: Here's my second question. If you lived on Mars, what would you miss most about Earth? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: If you lived on Mars, what would you miss most about Earth?

segments.text: So, could humans ever live on Mars? Maybe, but not on the surface as it is. You'd need a pressurized home, radiation shielding, and your own air, water and food.
segments.headline: A home on Mars?

segments.text: There's water, frozen in the polar ice caps and under the ground. It could give drinking water, oxygen, and even rocket fuel.

files: South Polar Cap of Mars during Martian South summer 2000.jpg
visual.query: South Polar Cap of Mars during Martian South summer 2000

segments.headline: Frozen water

segments.text: Could you make air there? Perseverance carried an experiment called MOXIE that turned Martian carbon dioxide into oxygen. Over two years it made about one hundred twenty grams. A tiny amount, but proof it can be done.
segments.headline: Making oxygen on Mars

segments.text: Food is harder. Martian soil has almost no nutrients and is laced with those toxic perchlorates. Crops would need sealed greenhouses, cleaned soil, and artificial light during dust storms.

files: Spanning the Delta of Jezero Crater on Mars (PIA25022).jpg
visual.query: Spanning the Delta of Jezero Crater on Mars (PIA25022)

segments.headline: Growing food

segments.text: Every breath, every meal, every drop would depend on machines. A single broken part could be deadly, with help seven months away.
So you'd never survive on Mars as you are. But with enough help, maybe one day, people will call it home.

files: Mars - August 30 2021 - Flickr - Kevin M. Gill.png
visual.query: Mars - August 30 2021 - Flickr - Kevin M. Gill

segments.headline: The verdict

segments.text: Want to see Mars yourself? On February nineteenth, twenty twenty-seven, Mars will be at opposition, rising at sunset and shining all night as a bright orange point. No telescope needed.

files: 2018 Night Sky Festival- Stargazing in the Meadow (44025262174).jpg
visual.query: 2018 Night Sky Festival- Stargazing in the Meadow (44025262174)

segments.headline: See it yourself

segments.text: And after all that, Earth, with its thick air, its liquid oceans and its magnetic shield, looks like the most precious place we know.
Now my last question. What should we never get close to next? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: What should we never get close to next?
